slides.headline: Six Children. Seven Years. One Confession.
slides.body: A bishop knew a father was abusing his kids. Arizona's Supreme Court just ruled he was right to stay silent.

slides.headline: Bisbee, Arizona. A Border Patrol Father.
slides.body: In 2011, Paul Adams confessed to Bishop John Herrod that he was molesting his 5-year-old daughter. Herrod called church leaders, not police.

slides.headline: Salt Lake City Told Him to Stay Silent.
slides.body: Church attorney Merrill Nelson told Herrod the confession was privileged. Adams confessed twice more. Abuse of six children continued seven more years.

slides.headline: The Court Ruled Unanimously. Every Justice.
slides.body: On July 30, 2026, Arizona's Supreme Court ruled churches, not judges, decide what counts as confession. The children's case was dismissed.

slides.headline: Every Faith Writes Its Own Exemption.
slides.body: From Catholic confessionals to Mormon bishops, states keep carving religious exemptions into child abuse law, protecting institutions, not children.

slides.headline: Whose Secret Was the Law Protecting?
slides.body: Six children paid for a confidentiality clause. Should any faith get to define its own exemption from reporting child abuse?
